match.reason: None of the bank points teaches how to structure a written analysis of a text's argument: they cover context, essay paragraph building, personal readings and logical flaws, so none matches this point's idea of introducing the issue and texts and then explaining how each part persuades.

draft.title: Writing the argument analysis
card: An argument analysis is about how a text persuades, not whether you agree with it. Write about the writer's choices and their effect on the audience.
Introduction
names the issue, the text, the writer, the form and the audience. It states the contention and the tone, and sums up how the writer tries to persuade.
Body paragraphs
follow the order of the argument, usually from start to finish. Each one covers a part of the argument, such as the opening, the evidence or the ending.
Inside a paragraph
name a technique, quote a few of the writer's words, then explain how it is meant to position the reader. Link back to the contention.
draft.remember: Introduce the issue and text, then follow the argument's order, explaining how each part persuades.

a.q: Which sentence from an argument analysis does the job of explaining persuasion?
opts: The vivid word "choked" is meant to make readers feel alarm
The writer says that city councils have ignored cyclists
The article was published in a newspaper on a Saturday
I disagree with the writer because bike lanes cost too much
a.why: This sentence names a choice, uses the writer's word and says how readers are meant to feel. The sentence about councils only retells what the writer says. The disagreement is the student's own opinion, which is not the task.
a.clue: Look for the choice and its effect on the reader.

b.q: Ravi is analysing an opinion piece. It opens with a story about a local pool, then gives figures, then ends with a call to sign a petition. How should his body paragraphs be ordered?
opts: Story, then figures, then the call to sign, each explained
Figures first as the strongest, then the story, then the call
One paragraph on all the techniques, then one on the tone
A paragraph on each technique, from his most to least liked
b.why: Body paragraphs follow the order of the argument, so each part is explained as the reader meets it. Starting with the strongest part or grouping by technique loses the way the argument builds.
b.clue: Which order matches how the reader meets the argument?
